speaker_policy: The recurring cast can often be inferred by a human, but the canonical artifact has no accepted named turns and no independently held-out multispeaker result. Named dialogue remains withheld.
source_notes: The archive calls this Episode 100, while the cast repeatedly calls it Episode 099¼, 099A or 099B and reserves the official hundredth celebration for Bobby Lee's return. Both numbering systems are retained.
The raw file contains 5,102 segments and approximately 31,241 words; the clean file contains 4,988 segments and approximately 31,261 words across 11,275.94 seconds.

The cleaner logs 104 empty artifacts and nineteen repeated-token items. Thirteen `empezar` tokens in the music-heavy intro and six terminal `All right` repetitions are degenerate runs; nine honest indistinct-audio spans explain why 123 logged edits produce a net 114-segment reduction.
The Alliance for California Traditional Arts independently documents Oakland's Korean Youth Cultural Center and its pungmul practice: https://actaonline.org/profile/korean-youth-cultural-center/
David Choe's own site preserves the Parts Unknown Koreatown/Sizzler appearance: https://davidchoe.com/2013/parts-unknown-david-choe-and-anthony-bourdain-at-sizzler
YouTube's official 2013 award video confirms Girls' Generation's `I Got a Boy` won Video of the Year: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=50RKQp_o4Jg

Contemporaneous Korean reporting supports the 1997 Meg Ryan / Sexy Mild / David Letterman controversy, while the episode's claim about Tommy Hilfiger making an anti-Black statement on Oprah is a debunked rumor.

The episode's racial, sexual, violent, coercive, factually wrong and self-contradictory ideas remain represented. Restrictions protect private people, intimate images and re-identifying details, not ideas.
summary: The archive's Episode 100 is deliberately not the cast's official Episode 100. They call it 099¼, 099A and 099B, reserving the milestone for Bobby Lee's return. That numbering conflict is itself useful provenance. The opening continues the Ranch record: David tried to regiment isolation into painting and reading, removed phone, television and porn, then describes how restriction redirected attention toward compulsive searching and masturbation. A proposed hundredth-episode concept remains secret because both this episode and the prior one explicitly link premature podcast disclosure to sabotage. The title section is an unstable mixture of stereotype, immigrant autobiography and real cultural history. David moves from Crown Royal, piano, violin, golf, Sizzler, fried chicken, coffee and Korean entertainment into his alienation from both Korean and non-Korean peers. The strongest primary account is not the list but the Oakland turn: hearing pungmul through a window, asking to join Korean Youth Cultural Center performers who spoke little English, returning until accepted, and playing community events for small fees. That practice gave him a form of Korean belonging he had not found through ordinary social identity. The archive preserves the surrounding anti-Korean generalizations and the reductive account of the 1992 Los Angeles uprising as attributed ideas while correcting them separately. It also resolves the Parts Unknown/Sizzler story, the Meg Ryan Sexy Mild controversy, Girls' Generation's 2013 YouTube award, TOM N TOMS, Paris Baguette, Oldboy and Daniel Wu. Later sections repeatedly test consent. David recommends strategic insincerity to obtain sex; a porn-as-visual-aid discussion sometimes treats a partner's curiosity as permission; the cast returns to a reported sleeping-person penetration from Episode 099; and robot rape fantasies blur programmed role-play with real consent. These are preserved without being converted into advice. Steve Lee's explicit refusal controls the proposed RealDoll gift even when the cast thinks overriding him would be funny. David's artificial-companion discussion connects Her and Black Mirror's Be Right Back to a wish for low-friction intimacy and eventually jealousy over a person who does not exist. The final hour is a Ranch-written Trivia with Choe homage. It is valuable as an index of callbacks and a demonstration of how the show elevates its own cast beside public figures, but many answers are wrong: A History of Violence, not Eastern Promises, is Viggo Mortensen's first major post-trilogy feature; Elijah Wood's post-trilogy chronology does not begin with Sin City; and the Korean YouTube/`Get Lucky` plagiarism clip is not proof. Named dialogue remains withheld.
